questions.question: Which test tube represents the result when cyclohexene is shaken with bromine water?
questions.answer: **B.** The bromine is consumed by addition, leaving two colourless immiscible layers.

questions.question: When is equilibrium reached in a reversible reaction?
options: When molecules of reactants cease to change into molecules of products.
When the concentrations of reactants and products are equal.
When the concentrations of reactants and products are constant.
When the activation energies of the forward and reverse reactions are equal.
questions.answer: **C.** Forward and reverse rates are equal, so concentrations stay constant.

questions.question: Which acid/base pair could act as a buffer?
questions.answer: **D.** A weak acid and its conjugate base.

Which reagent could be used to distinguish between primary, secondary and tertiary alcohols?
questions.answer: **B.** In the Lucas test tertiary alcohols turn cloudy at once, secondary slowly and primary hardly at all. Oxidants do not separate primary from secondary by observation.

questions.question: Under which conditions is a chemical reaction most likely to be spontaneous?
options: entropy decreasing, enthalpy decreasing, Gibbs free energy not relevant
questions.answer: **B.** $\Delta G=\Delta H-T\Delta S<0$ is guaranteed when $\Delta H<0$ and $\Delta S>0$.

questions.question: Consider the compounds W $\text{CH}_3\text{COOCH}_3$, X $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{NH}_2$, Y $\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}$ and Z $\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{OH}$. Which best describes them?

questions.question: Which combination produces the solution with the greatest temperature change?
questions.answer: **A.** $\Delta T$ depends on moles of water formed per volume: A forms 0.020 mol in 150 mL, far more per mL than the others.

questions.question: For the equilibrium $2\text{SO}_2(g)+\text{O}_2(g)\rightleftharpoons2\text{SO}_3(g)$, $\Delta H=-197$ kJ mol$^{-1}$. Explain the conditions of temperature and pressure that will increase the yield.
questions.answer:
**Low temperature:** the forward reaction is exothermic, so lowering the temperature shifts the equilibrium right to release heat (the reverse, endothermic rate falls more than the forward rate). Yield rises, although the reaction is slower.

**High pressure:** there are 3 moles of gas on the left and 2 on the right, so raising the pressure shifts the equilibrium towards fewer gas molecules (right). In collision terms, the forward collision frequency increases more than the reverse.

questions.question: For the equilibrium $2\text{SO}_2(g)+\text{O}_2(g)\rightleftharpoons2\text{SO}_3(g)$, $\Delta H=-197$ kJ mol$^{-1}$. Explain any effect on the equilibrium constant if the temperature is increased.
questions.answer: $K=\dfrac{[\text{SO}_3]^2}{[\text{SO}_2]^2[\text{O}_2]}$. Raising the temperature favours the endothermic reverse reaction, so $[\text{SO}_3]$ falls and the reactant concentrations rise: **$K$ decreases**.

questions.question: For each of reactions I, II and III in the scheme, identify the type of reaction and the reagents and conditions required.
questions.answer:
**I: substitution** (hydrolysis): aqueous NaOH or KOH, heat.

**II: esterification** (condensation): ethanoic acid, concentrated $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ catalyst, heat under reflux.

**III: dehydration** (elimination): concentrated $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ (or $\text{H}_3\text{PO}_4$) catalyst, heat.

A solution contains $\text{Ba}^{2+}$, $\text{Pb}^{2+}$ and $\text{Fe}^{2+}$. A student separated them using the flowchart, with only concentrated hydrochloric acid and concentrated ammonia solution. Identify the isolated products A, B and C, explaining your reasoning with observations where appropriate.
questions.answer:
Reagent 1 must be HCl (ammonia first would not separate the ions cleanly), and reagent 2 ammonia.

- **A:** white precipitate of $\text{PbCl}_2$; barium and iron(II) chlorides remain dissolved.
- **B:** green iron(II) precipitate, $\text{Fe(OH)}_2$, formed with ammonia (the flowchart labels it "metal complex").

questions.question: A compound $\text{C}_4\text{H}_8\text{Cl}_2$ is either 2,2-dichlorobutane or 2,3-dichlorobutane. Draw (give the structures of) the two isomers.
questions.answer: 2,2-dichlorobutane: $\text{CH}_3\text{CCl}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$. 2,3-dichlorobutane: $\text{CH}_3\text{CHClCHClCH}_3$.

questions.question: A compound $\text{C}_4\text{H}_8\text{Cl}_2$ is either 2,2-dichlorobutane or 2,3-dichlorobutane. Using the $^1$H and $^{13}$C NMR spectra shown, justify which isomer was produced, comparing the expected number of signals and splitting patterns.
questions.answer:
**$^1$H NMR** shows three signals: a singlet (about 2.2 ppm), a quartet (1.8 ppm) and a triplet (0.9 ppm). 2,2-dichlorobutane predicts exactly this: an isolated $\text{CH}_3$ (singlet) and a coupled $\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$ (quartet and triplet). 2,3-dichlorobutane is symmetrical and would give only two signals (a doublet and a multiplet).

**$^{13}$C NMR** shows four signals, including one far downfield (about 93 ppm) for a carbon bearing two Cl atoms. 2,3-dichlorobutane would give only two signals.

The product is **2,2-dichlorobutane**.

questions.question:
For $2\text{FeS}_2(s)+5\text{O}_2(g)\rightarrow2\text{FeO}(s)+4\text{SO}_2(g)$:

| | $\text{FeS}_2(s)$ | $\text{O}_2(g)$ | FeO(s) | $\text{SO}_2(g)$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| $\Delta H_f$ (kJ mol$^{-1}$) | −178 | 0 | −272 | −297 |

Use Hess's law to calculate the enthalpy change for the reaction.
questions.answer: $\Delta H=\sum\Delta H_f(\text{products})-\sum\Delta H_f(\text{reactants})=[2(-272)+4(-297)]-[2(-178)+0]=-1376$ kJ.

questions.question:
For $2\text{FeS}_2(s)+5\text{O}_2(g)\rightarrow2\text{FeO}(s)+4\text{SO}_2(g)$:

|---|---|---|---|---|
| $\Delta H_f$ (kJ mol$^{-1}$) | −178 | 0 | −272 | −297 |

Explain any changes in entropy as the reaction proceeds.
questions.answer: The number of moles of gas falls from 5 to 4, so the system becomes less disordered: **entropy decreases**.

questions.question: 20.00 mL of 0.10 mol L$^{-1}$ acetic acid in a conical flask was titrated with sodium hydroxide solution, giving the curve shown. Calculate and explain the concentration of hydrogen ions at positions A (start) and B (equivalence point) on the graph. Support your answer with TWO relevant equations.
questions.answer:
**A:** pH ≈ 3, so $[\text{H}^+]\approx10^{-3}$ mol L$^{-1}$. Acetic acid is weak and only partially ionises, so $[\text{H}^+]$ is much less than 0.10:
$$\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}+\text{H}_2\text{O}\rightleftharpoons\text{CH}_3\text{COO}^-+\text{H}_3\text{O}^+$$

**B:** pH ≈ 9, so $[\text{H}^+]\approx10^{-9}$ mol L$^{-1}$. The solution is sodium acetate, and the acetate ion is a weak base:
$$\text{CH}_3\text{COO}^-+\text{H}_2\text{O}\rightleftharpoons\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}+\text{OH}^-$$
The extra $\text{OH}^-$ makes the solution basic, with $[\text{H}^+]$ below $10^{-7}$.

questions.question: A brass zipper was dissolved in 20 mL of concentrated nitric acid and made up to 250 mL. Standards diluted from copper(II) nitrate gave the AAS calibration curve shown. The sample solution gave an absorbance of 0.72, so it was diluted to half its concentration. Explain why the sample solution was diluted.
questions.answer: 0.72 is above the highest standard, outside the range of the calibration curve. Linearity cannot be assumed there, so the result would not be valid. Halving the concentration brings it within range.

questions.question: A brass zipper was dissolved in 20 mL of concentrated nitric acid and made up to 250 mL. Standards diluted from copper(II) nitrate gave the AAS calibration curve shown. The sample solution gave an absorbance of 0.72, so it was diluted to half its concentration. The zipper had a mass of 1.62 g and the absorbance of the halved sample was 0.36. Calculate the percentage by mass of copper.
questions.answer:
From the curve, absorbance 0.36 corresponds to 0.034 mol L$^{-1}$, so the original solution was 0.068 mol L$^{-1}$.

$n=0.068\times0.250=0.017$ mol; $m=0.017\times63.55=1.08$ g.

$\%\text{Cu}=\dfrac{1.08}{1.62}\times100=67\%$.

questions.question: Determine the solubility, in grams per millilitre, of sodium sulfate heptahydrate in distilled water, given its solubility product constant is 17.67. $\text{Na}_2\text{SO}_4\cdot7\text{H}_2\text{O}(s)\rightleftharpoons2\text{Na}^+(aq)+\text{SO}_4^{2-}(aq)+7\text{H}_2\text{O}(l)$
The solubility product of $\text{Na}_2\text{SO}_4\cdot7\text{H}_2\text{O}$ is 17.67. Explain whether 25 g of it can dissolve completely in 100 mL of distilled water.
questions.answer: 25 g is 0.0932 mol, giving $[\text{SO}_4^{2-}]=0.932$ M and $[\text{Na}^+]=1.86$ M. $Q=(1.86)^2(0.932)=3.2$. Since $Q<K_{sp}$ (17.67), **all of it dissolves** (the maximum is about 44 g per 100 mL).

Use IUPAC nomenclature to identify compounds A, B and C.
questions.answer: A: butane. B: propan-1-ol. C: ethanamide.

questions.question:
Three organic compounds have these properties:

| | Compound | Molar mass (g mol$^{-1}$) | Boiling point (°C) |
|---|---|---|---|
| A | straight-chain alkane | 58 | −1 |
| B | primary alcohol | 60 | 97 |
| C | primary amide | 59 | 210 |

Explain the different boiling points of A, B and C, using at least one labelled diagram.
questions.answer:
The molar masses are similar, so the differences come from the type and number of intermolecular forces.

- **A, butane:** non-polar; only weak dispersion forces, so very low boiling point.
- **B, propan-1-ol:** the polar O–H allows hydrogen bonding (plus dipole–dipole and dispersion), so much more energy is needed.
- **C, ethanamide:** a polar C=O and two N–H bonds let each molecule form several hydrogen bonds (two donors, and lone pairs on O as acceptors), giving the most extensive network and highest boiling point.

Diagram (hydrogen bonds shown as ⋯):

- alcohol: $\text{C}_3\text{H}_7-\overset{\delta-}{\text{O}}-\overset{\delta+}{\text{H}}\cdots\overset{\delta-}{\text{O}}(\text{H})-\text{C}_3\text{H}_7$
- amide: $\text{CH}_3\text{C(NH}_2)=\overset{\delta-}{\text{O}}\cdots\overset{\delta+}{\text{H}}-\text{NH}-\text{C(O)CH}_3$

questions.question: In organic chemistry, oxidation and reduction are opposing reactions. Ethanal is reduced to product X and oxidised to product Y, as shown. Identify X and Y and outline how chemical tests and instrumental techniques (infrared and carbon-13 NMR spectroscopy) could confirm their identities.
questions.answer:
**X = ethanol, Y = ethanoic acid.**

**Chemical tests:** Y turns blue litmus red and produces $\text{CO}_2$ with sodium carbonate. X gives neither result but turns acidified dichromate from orange to green and releases $\text{H}_2$ with sodium (dry sample).

**IR:** ethanal has C=O at 1680–1750 cm$^{-1}$. In X this disappears and a broad O–H (3230–3550) and C–O (1000–1300) appear. In Y the C=O remains, with a very broad O–H (2500–3000) and C–O.

**$^{13}$C NMR:** each shows two signals. Ethanal's C=O at 190–220 ppm is replaced in X by a C–O signal at 50–90 ppm; in Y the carbonyl signal appears at 160–185 ppm. The $\text{CH}_3$ signal stays at 5–40 ppm.

questions.question:
A manufacturer claimed that each antacid tablet was 99.9% magnesium carbonate. A 0.747 g tablet was placed in a flask and 20.0 mL of 0.996 mol L$^{-1}$ HCl added. After reaction the mixture was boiled for 10 minutes, 10.0 mL of water added, and the excess HCl titrated with 0.110 mol L$^{-1}$ NaOH using phenolphthalein. The average titre was 22.39 mL.

Calculate the moles of acid in excess after the first reaction.
questions.answer: $\text{HCl}+\text{NaOH}\rightarrow\text{NaCl}+\text{H}_2\text{O}$. $n(\text{HCl})_{excess}=n(\text{NaOH})=0.110\times0.02239=2.46\times10^{-3}$ mol.

questions.question:
A manufacturer claimed that each antacid tablet was 99.9% magnesium carbonate. A 0.747 g tablet was placed in a flask and 20.0 mL of 0.996 mol L$^{-1}$ HCl added. After reaction the mixture was boiled for 10 minutes, 10.0 mL of water added, and the excess HCl titrated with 0.110 mol L$^{-1}$ NaOH using phenolphthalein. The average titre was 22.39 mL.

Determine the percentage of magnesium carbonate in the tablet and assess the manufacturer's claim.
questions.answer:
$\text{MgCO}_3+2\text{HCl}\rightarrow\text{MgCl}_2+\text{H}_2\text{O}+\text{CO}_2$

$n(\text{HCl added})=0.0200\times0.996=0.01992$; reacted $=0.01992-0.00246=0.01746$ mol.

$n(\text{MgCO}_3)=0.008729$ mol; $m=0.008729\times84.32=0.736$ g.

$\%=\dfrac{0.736}{0.747}\times100=98.5\%$. This is below the claimed 99.9%, so the claim is not supported (assuming only $\text{MgCO}_3$ reacts with the acid).

questions.question: A solution contains 6.0 mol L$^{-1}$ ammonium chloride and 0.40 mol L$^{-1}$ ammonia. At 25 °C, $K_a(\text{NH}_4^+)=6.3\times10^{-10}$. Assume ammonium chloride dissociates completely. Write a net ionic equation for the reaction of ammonium chloride with water.
questions.answer: $\text{NH}_4^+(aq)+\text{H}_2\text{O}(l)\rightleftharpoons\text{NH}_3(aq)+\text{H}_3\text{O}^+(aq)$

questions.question: A solution contains 6.0 mol L$^{-1}$ ammonium chloride and 0.40 mol L$^{-1}$ ammonia. At 25 °C, $K_a(\text{NH}_4^+)=6.3\times10^{-10}$. Assume ammonium chloride dissociates completely. Write the $K_a$ expression for the ammonium ion.
questions.answer: $K_a=\dfrac{[\text{NH}_3][\text{H}_3\text{O}^+]}{[\text{NH}_4^+]}$
